title: Recommendations for Revising the Open Access Classification System in OpenAlex | Zenodo
content: "The open access (OA) color classification system used by Unpaywall (i.e., Gold, Green, Hybrid, Bronze, and closed) was introduced in 2018 and has since become widely used across the ecosystem, including by Scopus, Web of Science, Dimensions, and numerous funders and institutions worldwide. However, the scholarly communication landscape has changed significantly since these categories were defined and the limits of this system are proving problematic. In particular, the current system struggles with research outputs that are not journal publications, relies too heavily on journal-level policies rather than work-level attributes, conflates business models with access status, and is difficult to accurately operationalize in an environment where journals regularly change the OA status of publications en masse. The OpenAlex Colors Working Group was convened by the OpenAlex Community Advisory Board in January 2026 to evaluate these limitations and recommend a revised framework. title: A beginner’s guide to open science | THE Campus Learn, Share, Connect
content:
"You might’ve come across words like “transparency” or “reproducibility” in the past few years. Perhaps you’ve overheard colleagues talking about data sharing or preregistering a study plan. If you aren’t familiar with open science, it can sound like a collection of jargon or buzzwords. 

However, open science is best understood as both a set of research practices and a broader commitment to making the processes by which scientific knowledge is produced more transparent, accessible and open to scrutiny."

title: Biomedical Publishing Metrics as a Barrier to Knowledge Dissemination
content: Abstract:  The Journal Impact Factor (JIF) is an outdated biomedical metric that hinders knowledge dissemination. Relying on citation counts creates a skewed, easily manipulated system with a temporal lag that ignores global equity. Frontline clinicians consume research to improve care but rarely generate citations, meaning the JIF cannot capture real-world clinical utility. To ensure rankings reflect true value, publishers must adopt a multi-dimensional matrix prioritizing usage-based Altmetrics, such as verified downloads and views, to instantly measure global clinical application.

title: Unlocking knowledge: diamond open access publishing - UNESCO Digital Library
content: Diamond Open Access (OA) is an equitable scholarly publishing model that treats knowledge as a digital public good, with no fees for readers or authors. Built on shared infrastructure, open licensing, and community governance, it supports non-profit, academically driven publishing while allowing commercial providers to deliver specific services. Like Open Educational Resources (OER), Diamond OA promotes equitable access, collaboration, and multilingual knowledge sharing. It can strengthen national and institutional Open Access strategies while connecting OER, Open Data, and open research software into interoperable knowledge ecosystems. This brief examines Diamond OA infrastructure and provides practical policy guidance for Member States and institutions.

title: From access to impact: the gold OA advantage | Springer Nature
content:
"This white paper explores the effect of different routes to OA on the reach and impact of articles in hybrid journals. The data shows that, 8 years on from our first major study into this topic, there is still a substantial advantage for gold OA articles across all disciplines (measured by downloads, citations and Altmetric Attention Score) over both non-OA articles and green OA articles. 4

The analysis of 204,781 articles published in 1,812 hybrid Springer Nature journals in 2023 also shows how gold OA can accelerate the number of downloads over time and the diversity of geographic readership, leading to faster impact and greater equity in access."

title: Gold OA reaches record 44pc share of global research output - Research Information
content:
"Gold open access (OA) articles reached their highest-ever share of global research output in 2025, accounting for 44% of all journal articles, reviews and conference papers published worldwide.

Nearly two million research articles were published through gold OA during the year, making it the principal driver of immediate, freely available access to research, according to the latest release of the STM Open Access Dashboard.

The Dashboard, which tracks the uptake of different routes to OA between 2015 and 2025, shows that gold OA has quadrupled over the past decade."

title: Open Access Library and Information Science (LIS) Journals Indexed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ): An Analytical Study | Annals of Library and Information Studies
content: Abstract: The study examines the trends and current status of Open Access (OA) research journals listed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) in the field of Library and Information Science (LIS) from 2003 to mid-2026. It investigates the profile of OA LIS journals, publishing trends, publishing practices, open access policies, licensing practices and journal scope through thematic analysis of keywords. The study identified 231 OA LIS journals published in 32 languages by 200 publishers across 55 countries globally. The study adopted a descriptive research approach and data were collected from the DOAJ and verified through the official journal websites where required. The collected data were compiled, organised, tabulated and analysed using Microsoft Excel. The findings provide insights into the growth of LIS journals, geographical distribution, publishers, language profile, publication mode, peer-review practices, article processing charges (APCs), copyright ownership, Creative Commons licensing, self-archiving policies, digital preservation mechanisms, Digital Object Identifier (DOI) availability and other publishing infrastructure adopted by OA LIS journals.

title: Perceived ease of access and use of open access resources by library and information science postgraduate students in south-west Nigeria
content: Abstract: Thi study examined Perceived Ease of Access (PEOA) and Use of Open Access Resources (OAR) by Library and Information Science (LIS) postgraduate students in universities in Southwest, Nigeria. The study adopted a quantitative research method and correlational research design to answer two research questions and one hypothesis. The population consisted of 227 postgraduate students from five universities: Adeleke University (AU) - 22, Babcock University (BU)-35, Lead City University (LCU)-30, Tai Solarin University (TASUED)-30 and University of Ibadan (UI)-110. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire administered through the total enumeration technique. The collected data were analysed using both descriptive and inferential statistical methods. The findings revealed that the largest respondents were: UI (49%), females (50.7%), age group 26-30 (39.4%), and single (55.9%). OARs were used mostly for research work (=3.60); group/individual practical purposes (=3.34) personal tutorials (=3.26) and examination preparation (=3.24). title: Strengthening Trust and Leadership: Reflections on National Institutes of Health (NIH) 2026 Community Days: Securing NIH Controlled-Access Data and Our Data Protection Journey | Data Science at NIH
content: "On April 13 and 14, I had the privilege of leading the National Institutes of Health (NIH) 2026 Community Days: Securing NIH Controlled-Access Data webinars to engage directly with our stakeholders, researchers, and the broader public about the critical work we’re undertaking to protect controlled-access data. These sessions were designed to foster transparency around our security and operational standards, update the community on new resources and requirements, and reinforce our shared responsibility in safeguarding participant trust. I am deeply grateful for the vibrant participation and thoughtful questions that were raised, which underscores the importance and urgency of our mission. Protecting participants’ trust requires one standard: secure, consistent protections for NIH controlled-access data—whether it is processed within a NIH Controlled-Access Data Repository (CADR) or a research institution’s IT systems. This principle drove the Extramural Community Days agenda, where we discussed not only what needs to be done, but why rigorous data protection is more essential than ever. Our commitment goes beyond compliance; it’s about honoring the trust participants place in us

title: New Guidelines Created for Publishing Indigenous Data | Dartmouth
content:
"To ensure that Indigenous peoples’ rights and knowledge are recognized in scientific data and scholarly publishing, a team of Indigenous scholars led by Lydia Jennings, an assistant professor of environmental studies, has established Guidelines for the Governance of Indigenous Peoples’ Data in Scholarly Publishing.

The guidelines (PDF) seek to implement the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance in the publishing realm. CARE is an acronym that stands for collective benefit, authority to control data, responsibility, and ethics."
